accuracy.evidence: Placement checked against DfE Development Matters 2021, Reception Writing ('spell words by identifying the sounds and then writing the sound with letter/s'; 'write short sentences with words with known sound-letter correspondences using a capital letter and full stop') and the EYFS ELG Writing. Definitions match common Reception usage: a label is a single naming word placed by the thing it names; a caption is a short sentence about the picture with a capital and a full stop; labels take no full stop. Every lab item checked by hand: dog = d-o-g and hat = h-a-t (3 phonemes, 3 graphemes each, Phase 2 CVC words), the six sort cards (3 one-word labels, 3 full sentences), the caption order The dog is in the sun. with only the first word capitalised, and the 5 robot cases (2 right, 3 slips). Parameterised answers (a, b, a and a+b) stay between 1 and 6 at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips Reception teachers report for labelling: writing only the initial sound ('d' for dog: Done-early feedback in Sound it out, robot case 3, m2, challenge 'first'), random or copied letters instead of listening (wrong-letter feedback names whether the sound is in the word at all, m4, challenge 'copy'), a label put by the wrong thing (Label it drop feedback, robot case 2, m7, challenge 'where'), mixing labels with captions (Label or caption sort feedback, m1, m8, challenge 'label'/'story'), a caption with no capital or full stop (Make a caption refuses lower-case 'the' first and an early full stop, robot case 4, m3, challenge 'caps'/'order') and a full stop on a one-word label (p3, m6, challenge 'dotlabel').

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglabel is about writing for a picture: the child drags word cards onto the thing each one names and a line snaps to it, writes dog and hat by tapping one letter per sound into three boxes (with a Done key that catches first-sound-only labels), drags single cards into Label or Caption bins, orders seven word tiles including The/the and the full stop into a caption, and judges a robot's labels and caption. flagmyname copies one known name from a card, flagpic reads labels and captions in books, and the segmenting lab splits spoken words; none places labels on a picture or builds a caption. The lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds the rules by doing: a label dropped on the wrong thing bounces back with 'This label says sun. That is the tree', the letter boxes only fill in sound order so the child must say d-o-g, pressing Done after one letter says how many sounds are still missing, each sort mistake names why the card is a label or a caption, and the caption tiles refuse lower-case 'the' first and a full stop in the middle. The done messages state each rule only after the task is complete.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab then disproves: 'A long story about the picture' (the labels the child places are single words), 'Write the first letter, d' (the dog label needs all three boxes before it counts), 'A label' for The dog is in the sun. (the sorter files whole sentences as captions), and 'Yes, d is enough' (the robot's 'd' label is a slip with its own fix).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with its own slip and message: story ('A label is not a story'), where ('goes next to the thing it names, with a line to it'), label, caps ('starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop'), first ('a letter for every sound, not just the first one'), copy ('Any letters will not say the word'), order and dotlabel ('A label ... does not need a full stop'). In-lab feedback also names the slip: the wrong thing, a sound not in the word, a sound not yet due, too few sounds, capital and full-stop placement.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short sentences with words like label, word, sound, letter, picture, capital and full stop; the adult text names the curriculum lines and key words plainly; validate_lessons readability passes for both. Canvas banners are short ('Put each label by the thing it names', 'Tap the words in order to make the caption') and every card word is read aloud through the live region when tapped, for children who cannot read it yet.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence is a rule or an example (one word that names a thing, say it slowly, a letter for each sound, a caption tells about the whole picture, capital and full stop, no full stop on a label); the adult paragraphs give placement and key words, how to segment and accept plausible spellings, the common mistakes, and what each lab scene does. The content gate finds no filler phrases.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark for every scene before and after Show me: the three word cards are about 100 px wide, the sun, tree and cat are about 60 px and spaced across the width, the letter tiles are about 60 px with 26 px letters, the Label and Caption bins sit side by side with short sub-labels that fit, the seven caption tiles wrap to two rows, and banners fit on one line. A Playwright drag on an iPhone 13 viewport placed sun, cat and tree and sorted a card into Label.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: pick a label then 'Put by the sun/tree/cat', each letter tile ('Letter d') plus Done, Label and Caption, each caption word ('word The', 'full stop'), Right and Slip. Tapping a card reads its word aloud through the live region, the canvas aria-label follows every message, and the walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
